uncited: Central difference stencils approximate the partial derivative of a scalar field at a voxel center by computing the difference between field values at symmetric neighbors, divided by twice the step size.
This method is second-order accurate, offering higher precision than forward or backward differences for smooth fields, at the cost of requiring samples from both sides of the evaluation point.
It is the standard baseline for gradient computation in volume rendering when analytic gradients are unavailable or too expensive to compute.

All methods in this family approximate the partial derivative $\frac{\partial V}{\partial x_i}$ at a voxel center $\mathbf{p}$ using a linear combination of scalar field values $V(\mathbf{p}_k)$ at neighboring positions $\mathbf{p}_k$.
where $w_k$ are weights determined by the stencil geometry and step size $h$ (voxel spacing).
For isotropic grids with $h=1$, the weights are typically integers or simple fractions.
The gradient vector is assembled as $\nabla V = (G_x, G_y, G_z)$.
Accurate central differencing requires tracing 6 additional rays per sample via infinitesimal rays to find containing regions, which is expensive.
Time complexity is $O(n)$ function evaluations without importance sampling (IS), $O(n)$ with IS, and $O(1)$ with Aggregate IS.
Central difference stencils are a fundamental numerical analysis technique widely used in scientific computing and computer graphics.
In the context of volume rendering, they are employed to estimate surface normals or density gradients from discrete voxel data when analytic derivatives are not available.
